title: 8 Key Data Structures That Power Modern Databases

segments.text: In this video, we uncovered a secret behind the modern databases we know and love.
From my sequel to Redis to Cassandra, we break down the eight essential data structures
that make it all possible.
Next I write in.
First up is skip list.
A skip list is a probabilistic data structure that is used to implement a sort of set.
It is an alternative to a balanced tree.
This allows for efficient search, insertion, and deletion operations.
In an in-memory database like Redis, a skip list is used to implement the order,
data structure, such as sort of set.
It allows for fast lookups, range queries, and other operations.
Next is hash index.
A hash index, also known as a hash table, is used to efficiently map keys to values
by using a hash function to generate a hash value for each key.
The hash value is used to quickly locate the value in the table, allowing for fast lookups,
insertions, and deletions.
Hash index is ubiquitous.
This obviously is used to implement hash data structures by hashes in Redis,
but is also widely used internally in all kinds of databases.
The next two data structures go hand in hand.
The SS table and the LSM tree.
SS table or sort of string table.
It is used to store data on disk in a sort of order.
It is a file-based data structure that is used to store large amounts of data
in a highly compressed and efficient format.
SS table is a core component of the LSM tree.
The other core component is a map table.
Mamm table is an in-memory data structure that stores recent rights.
SS table and Mamm table work together to handle a high volume of right operations.
We have an entire video dedicated to the LSM tree.
Check out the description below for a link to the video.
LSM tree is the backbone of popular and no-secret databases,
such as Apache's Cassandra, Rockstab and LevelDB.
Next up is the B tree family.
We include the B plus tree in this.
The B tree family of data structures are used to efficiently store and retrieve large amounts of data on disk.
B tree is a balance tree where each node can have multiple children and keeps data sorted.
B plus tree is a specific type of B tree where all data is stored in leaf notes and internal notes only whole keys.
They are widely used in databases such as mySQL, Postgres, and Oracle to handle large amounts of on this data.
Next is inverter index.
An inverter index is usually efficiently searched and retrieve data from a large collection of text documents.
You create a mapping of words to documents in which they appear.
The index is inverted because it maps the words to the documents rather than the other way around.
Inverter indexes are commonly used in documents search engines by elastic search.
Next is suffix tree.
It is used in databases for efficient text searching.
You quickly find all occurrences of a search term within a large collection of documents.
The last data structure will discuss is somewhat specialized.
It is archery.
An archery is a spatial index data structure that organizes data based on their geometric boundaries, such as rectangles or polygons.
It is used to efficiently store and retrieve spatial data in a database.
It allows for fast spatial queries and is widely used in spatial databases that post GIS, MongoDB, and Elastic Search.
This concludes our discussion of the eight data structures that power a modern data basis.
This is by no mean and exhaustive list.
Please let us know if there are others you would like us to discuss in the future.
